summary: The TRILL RBridge Channel mechanism from RFC 7178 allows typed messages between TRILL switches in the same campus and between switches and end stations on the same link. This proposed standard extends the RBridge Channel header so it can carry more information.

plainLanguage.summary: TRILL switches need a way to send each other small control messages, such as link-failure notifications, and the RBridge Channel is the mechanism for that. This RFC extends it in two ways: it lets one control message carry another kind of message inside it, and it lets the sender protect what it is carrying with encryption and a check that nobody has tampered with it.

subtitle: Tunnelling and securing the typed messages that TRILL switches send to each other.

tldr.problem: The RBridge Channel facility lets TRILL switches exchange typed messages, but the original design has no standard way to carry a payload of another kind inside such a message, and no way to protect the message at all.
tldr.mechanism: This document extends the RBridge Channel header with a Channel Protocol value that marks the extension, and adds four fields: a payload type, a security type, a sub-error field and a reserved nibble. The extended header is followed by variable-length security information and by the tunnelled data itself.
tldr.outcome: A TRILL switch can now carry an RBridge Channel message, a TRILL data packet, a TRILL IS-IS packet or a whole Ethernet frame inside an RBridge Channel message, and can protect the payload with DTLS, with the IS-IS authentication mechanism, or with both. The RFC recommends DTLS pairwise security and composite security, and warns that accepting tunnelled payloads too liberally is a risk.

today: RFC 7978 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2016. It updates RFC 7178, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or further updates it. It builds on the TRILL base protocol in RFC 6325 and its clarifications in RFC 7780.

sections.title: What This Document Adds to the RBridge Channel
sections.content:
The TRILL base protocol has been extended with the RBridge Channel facility to support the transmission of typed messages, for example Bidirectional Forwarding Detection, between two TRILL switches in the same campus, and the transmission of such messages between RBridges and end stations on the same link. Between two RBridges in the same campus, a TRILL data packet with a TRILL header is used and the destination RBridge is indicated by nickname. Between a RBridge and an end station on the same link, in either direction, a native RBridge Channel message with no TRILL header is used and the destination port is indicated by a MAC address.

This document updates RFC 7178 and specifies extensions to the RBridge Channel header that provide two additional facilities. The first is a standard method to tunnel payloads, whose type may be indicated by Ethertype, through encapsulation in RBridge Channel messages. The second is a method to provide security facilities for RBridge Channel messages. The example uses requiring such facilities are the security of Pull Directory messages, address flush messages and port shutdown messages.

Use of each facility is optional, except that if the header extension is implemented, two payload types must be implemented. Both facilities can be used in the same packet. In case of conflict between this document and RFC 7178, this document takes precedence.
sections.plainLanguage: RBridge Channel is the pipe TRILL switches use to send each other control messages. Before this RFC the pipe could carry only one kind of content, and that content was unprotected. The extension adds both a way to carry something else inside the pipe and a way to lock it.

sections.title: The Extended Header Layout
sections.content:
The RBridge Channel header carries the Ethertype 0x8946, a Channel Header Version field, a Channel Protocol field that gives the type of RBridge Channel message and says how to interpret the payload, and then Flags and ERR fields. This document is based on RBridge Channel version zero.

The extensions are themselves an RBridge Channel protocol, the Extended RBridge Channel Protocol. The Channel Protocol field is set to the value allocated for this purpose, 0x004, and the extension adds four more fields after the Flags and ERR fields: SubERR, a 4-bit field that gives further detail when an error is indicated in the ERR field and must be sent as zero otherwise; RESV4, a 4-bit field that must be sent as zero and is an error condition if it is not; SType, which describes the type of security information and features being used or provided; and PType, the payload type describing the tunnelled data.

After the extended header come the Security Information, which is variable length and of length zero when SType is zero, and then the Tunneled Data, also variable length. Using an RBridge Channel protocol to indicate extensions makes it easy to determine whether a remote RBridge supports them, because RBridges advertise in their link state packets which such protocols they support. Extension errors are reported as if they were RBridge Channel errors, using newly allocated code points in the ERR field supplemented by the SubERR field.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension works by claiming a new protocol number in the existing header, so that a switch that has not heard of the extension simply ignores the message. Inside that claim the header gains four small fields: what kind of payload follows, what kind of protection was applied, a detail code for errors, and one reserved field that must be zero.

sections.title: Payload Types
sections.content:
The PType field says what the tunneled data is. PType 0 and PType 15 are reserved, PType 1 is the Null payload, PType 2 is an Ethertyped payload, PType 3 is an Ethernet frame, and PType 4 to 14 are unassigned. While implementation of the header extension is optional, if it is implemented, PType 1 and PType 2 with the RBridge-Channel Ethertype must be implemented; PType 2 for other Ethertypes and PType 3 may be implemented.

The Null payload indicates that there is no user data payload, and is intended for testing or for messages such as key negotiation where only security information is present. Any tunnelled user data after the Security Information field is ignored.

PType 2 means the payload begins with an Ethertype. A payload beginning with the RBridge-Channel Ethertype is an encapsulated RBridge Channel message, and a typical reason for doing that is to provide security services such as authentication or encryption for the encapsulated message. A payload beginning with the TRILL Ethertype is an encapsulated TRILL data packet, which, if the Ethertype is supported and the message meets local policy, is handled as if it had been received by the destination switch on the port where the extended message arrived. A payload beginning with the L2-IS-IS Ethertype is an encapsulated TRILL IS-IS packet, which one possible use of which is to expedite the receipt of a link state packet by switches with an immediate need for that information.

PType 3 means the payload is an Ethernet frame as might be received from or sent to an end station, except that the frame's FCS is omitted. The priority of the RBridge Channel message can be copied from the frame's VLAN tag if one is present, except that priority 7 should only be used for messages critical to establishing or maintaining adjacency, and priority 6 only for other important control messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Three kinds of content can be carried: nothing at all, which is useful when the message is only about security; something that starts with a type code saying what protocol it is; or a complete Ethernet frame. The point of the Ethertyped payload is that the same wrapping mechanism can carry an ordinary control message, a data packet, or a routing update.

sections.title: The Four Security Types
sections.content:
The SType field gives the type of security being used. SType 0 is None, where no security services are invoked and the Security Information field has length zero. SType 1 is IS-IS CRYPTO_AUTH-based authentication, which gives security similar to that provided for IS-IS packets by the IS-IS Authentication TLV, but provides only authentication, does not provide for key negotiation, and is therefore NOT RECOMMENDED. SType 2 is DTLS Pairwise Security, and SType 3 is Composite Security. The use of DTLS Pairwise Security or Composite Security is RECOMMENDED.

With DTLS Pairwise Security, the entire payload of the extended packet, starting just after the null Security Information and ending just before the link trailer, is one or more DTLS records. DTLS records must be limited by the path MTU so that each record fits entirely within a single extended RBridge Channel message. A minimum path MTU can be determined from the TRILL campus minimum MTU Sz, which will not be less than 1470 bytes, by allowing for the TRILL data packet, extended channel and DTLS framing overhead. The DTLS pairwise keying is set up between a pair of RBridges, independent of the Data Label, using messages of a priority configurable at the RBridge level, which defaults to priority 6.

Composite Security is the combination of DTLS Pairwise Security and IS-IS CRYPTO_AUTH-based authentication. On transmission the DTLS records are secured first and then used as the payload for the authentication. On reception the authentication is verified first and an error is returned if it fails, and only then are the DTLS records processed. The advantage is that the payload is authenticated and encrypted with a modern security protocol, and in addition the RBridge Channel header and, except in the native case, the preceding MAC addresses and Data Label get some authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four choices. No protection at all. Authentication borrowed from the routing protocol, which checks the message but does not hide it and cannot agree keys, so the RFC advises against it. DTLS, which does both and is recommended. And a combination of the two, where the routing protocol's check covers the header as well as the encrypted payload.

sections.title: Derived Keying Material
sections.content:
In some cases it is possible to use material derived from IS-IS CRYPTO_AUTH keying material as an element of Extended RBridge Channel security, on the assumption that the IS-IS keying material is of high quality. The material actually used is derived as HKDF-Expand-SHA256 applied to the IS-IS keying material, with the 16-character ASCII string "Extended Channel" concatenated with a single byte whose upper nibble is zero and whose lower nibble is the SType, and with the length of the output needed. The string is used without any leading length byte or trailing zero byte.

Because the IS-IS keying material might expire or be invalidated, the use of derived material from it must cease at the time of or before such expiration or invalidation. Continued security may use new derived material from currently valid IS-IS CRYPTO_AUTH keying material.

The SType 1 security information holds four reserved bits that must be sent as zero, a Size field set to two plus the size of the authentication data in bytes, a Key ID that specifies the keying value and authentication algorithm used for TRILL IS-IS authentication TLVs, and the authentication data itself. The keying material actually used is always the derived material. The authenticated area starts with the byte immediately after the TRILL header's optional flag word if it is present, or after the ingress nickname if it is not, and extends to just before the link trailer. In the native RBridge Channel case it starts with the RBridge-Channel Ethertype instead, because there is no TRILL header, inner Ethernet addresses or inner Data Label.
sections.plainLanguage: Rather than inventing a new set of keys, the extension can derive what it needs from the keys the routing protocol already uses. The derivation names the purpose in the string "Extended Channel" and the kind of protection in one byte, so that a key used for one purpose cannot be reused for another. When the routing keys are rotated or expire, the derived keys stop being used with them.

sections.title: Errors
sections.content:
Extension errors are reported like RBridge Channel errors, with the ERR field set to one of three new code points: 6 for an unknown or unsupported field value, 7 for an authentication failure, and 8 for an error in a nested RBridge Channel message.

When the ERR field is 6, the SubERR field says which field or value was the problem. SubERR 0 means no error, and suberrors are not allowed. SubERR 1 is a non-zero RESV4 nibble, 2 is an unsupported SType, 3 is an unsupported PType, 4 is an unknown Key ID, 5 is an unsupported Ethertype with PType 2, 6 is an unsupported authentication algorithm for SType 1, and 7 is a non-zero SubERR with a zero ERR field. At this time no suberror codes are assigned under any other ERR field value.

There is one special case for nested messages. If an extended RBridge Channel message is sent with security and with a payload type indicating an Ethertyped payload whose Ethertype indicates a nested RBridge Channel message, and there is an error in processing that nested message that results in a returned RBridge Channel message with a non-zero ERR field, then that returned message should also be nested in an extended RBridge Channel message using the same type of security, and the ERR field in the extended envelope is set to 8.
sections.plainLanguage: When something goes wrong the switch sets an error code, and a second field narrows it down to the particular field or value that caused the problem. If the failed message was itself wrapped inside another one, the error travels back in the same wrapping, so that the outer layer protects the error report too.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension has potentially positive and negative effects on security. On the positive side, it provides optional security that can be used to authenticate and/or encrypt RBridge Channel messages. Some RBridge Channel message payloads, such as BFD, provide their own security, but where this is not true, consideration should be given, when specifying an RBridge Channel protocol, to recommending or requiring use of the security features of the extension.

On the negative side, the optional ability to tunnel more payload types, and to tunnel them between TRILL switches and to and from end stations, can increase risk unless precautions are taken. The processing of decapsulated payloads is a place where an implementation should not be liberal in what it accepts, because the tunnelling facility makes it easier for unexpected messages to turn up in unexpected places in a campus, through accidents or the actions of an adversary. Local policies should generally be strict, and accept only payload types that are required, and then only with adequate security for the circumstances.

If IS-IS authentication is not being used, then IS-IS CRYPTO_AUTH keying material would not normally be available, but that presumably represents a judgment by the campus operator that no security is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives both sides of the ledger. The extension lets a campus protect its control traffic, which is a gain. It also lets a campus carry traffic it never carried before, and the RFC is blunt that a switch should refuse anything it does not actually need, because a wrapped message can arrive somewhere it was never meant to.

data.title: Fixed part of the extended header

fields.name: CHV
fields.desc: Channel Header Version. This document is based on version zero.

fields.name: Channel Protocol
fields.desc: 0x004 indicates that the header extension is present.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: The Flags field of the RBridge Channel Header.

fields.name: ERR
fields.desc: The error code. Zero means no error.

fields.name: SubERR
fields.desc: Further detail when an error is indicated. Must be sent as zero when ERR is zero.

fields.name: RESV4
fields.desc: Reserved. Must be sent as zero; a non-zero value on receipt is an error.

fields.name: SType
fields.desc: The security type: the kind of protection applied to the payload.

fields.name: PType
fields.desc: The payload type: what the tunnelled data is.

items.label: Null
items.desc: No user data payload. Used for testing or for messages such as key negotiation where only security information is present.

items.label: Ethertyped Payload
items.desc: The tunnelled data begins with an Ethertype. Support is required for the RBridge-Channel Ethertype and optional for others.

items.label: Ethernet Frame
items.desc: The tunnelled data is an Ethernet frame, with its FCS omitted.

items.label: None
items.desc: No security services are invoked. The Security Information field has length zero.

items.label: IS-IS CRYPTO_AUTH
items.desc: Authentication in the style of the IS-IS Authentication TLV. It provides no key negotiation, so its use is NOT RECOMMENDED.

items.label: DTLS Pairwise
items.desc: The whole payload is one or more DTLS records, encrypted and authenticated between a pair of RBridges. RECOMMENDED.

items.label: Composite
items.desc: DTLS pairwise security with the IS-IS authentication applied over it, so the header is authenticated as well. RECOMMENDED.

viz.caption: HOW THE KEY MATERIAL IS DERIVED

data.title: Derived keying material
data.code:
Derived Material =
   HKDF-Expand-SHA256 ( IS-IS-key, "Extended Channel" | 0x0S, L )

"Extended Channel" : the 16-character ASCII string,
                       with no leading length byte and no trailing zero byte
0x0S                 : one byte, upper nibble zero, lower nibble the SType
L                    : the length of the derived material needed
